steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on synthesizing training data for image recognition with generative models. Motivate why synthetic training data is attractive, explain the gap between synthetic and real data, present our distribution-matching framework and how we implement it with a text-to-image diffusion model, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why large annotated datasets matter and why collecting them is hard
- Prior work on training data synthesis with generative models, and the remaining gap
- Our theoretical framework: training data synthesis as distribution matching
- Implementation with Stable Diffusion and experimental results
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale annotated datasets are essential in deep learning for image recognition, because they give the comprehensive information that models need to discover patterns, learn representations, and make accurate predictions. But collecting such datasets by hand takes a lot of time and labor, and it can also cause privacy concerns. Because of these challenges, training data synthesis is a promising alternative to traditional data collection, either to augment the original real datasets or to replace them.

There are many image synthesis strategies, and deep generative models have received a lot of attention, mainly because they can produce high-fidelity images. Early studies used Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to synthesize annotated training data for image classification and segmentation. More recently, more works have focused on synthesizing training data with the powerful diffusion models, for self-supervised pre-training, transfer learning, domain generalization, and supervised image classification. However, even with all this research, there is still a notable performance gap between models trained on synthetic data and models trained on real data. One main reason for this gap is that the synthetic and real data distributions are misaligned, even when the diffusion model is trained on web-scale datasets, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Previous works have tried to fix this with heuristic-driven approaches like prompt engineering and with expensive inversion approaches, but these solutions are neither sufficient nor efficient. Also, there are no theoretical frameworks that can properly explain and analyze in a principled way why synthetic training data works.

- our framework: distribution-matching perspective on training data synthesis
  - from first principle of supervised learning, recast synthesis as distribution matching
  - two principles: (1) distribution discrepancy between target and synthetic data, (2) cardinality of the training set
- implementation on Stable Diffusion: refine training objectives, condition generation, prior initialization for better alignment
  - scenarios: (1) synthetic only, (2) augmenting real data, (3) scaling law
  - ImageNet1k + ResNet50: 1 \times synthetic -> 70.9% Top1; 10 \times -> 76.0%
  - OOD generalization and privacy preservation: promising
  - insights for refining the pipeline
- contributions: framework (two foundational aspects); diffusion-based synthesis strategy with component analysis; state of the art + OOD and privacy advantages

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale annotated datasets are essential in deep learning for image recognition, because they give the comprehensive information that models need to discover patterns, learn representations, and make accurate predictions. But collecting such datasets by hand takes a lot of time and labor, and it can also cause privacy concerns. Because of these challenges, training data synthesis is a promising alternative to traditional data collection, either to augment the original real datasets or to replace them.

There are many image synthesis strategies, and deep generative models have received a lot of attention, mainly because they can produce high-fidelity images. Early studies used Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to synthesize annotated training data for image classification and segmentation. More recently, more works have focused on synthesizing training data with the powerful diffusion models, for self-supervised pre-training, transfer learning, domain generalization, and supervised image classification. However, even with all this research, there is still a notable performance gap between models trained on synthetic data and models trained on real data. One main reason for this gap is that the synthetic and real data distributions are misaligned, even when the diffusion model is trained on web-scale datasets, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Previous works have tried to fix this with heuristic-driven approaches like prompt engineering and with expensive inversion approaches, but these solutions are neither sufficient nor efficient. Also, there are no theoretical frameworks that can properly explain and analyze in a principled way why synthetic training data works.

To improve the quality and utility of the synthetic training data produced by deep generative models, we present a theoretical framework for training data synthesis from a distribution-matching perspective. Specifically, we start from the first principle of supervised learning and recast training data synthesis as a distribution matching problem. This puts the emphasis on two primary principles of synthetic data: (1) The distribution discrepancy between target and synthetic data, and (2) The cardinality of the training set.

Based on this, we implement the framework on the state-of-the-art text-to-image diffusion model, Stable Diffusion, and we carefully analyze and refine the training objectives, the condition generation, and the prior initialization so that synthetic and target data distributions are better aligned. We validate our theoretical framework and synthesis method empirically on diverse benchmarks, which cover different scenarios: (1) training only with synthetic data, (2) augmenting the real training data, and (3) evaluating the scaling law between synthetic data and performance. In particular, for ImageNet1k classification with ResNet50, training only with synthetic data equivalent to 1 \times the original real data size gives 70.9% Top1 classification accuracy, and this goes up to 76.0% when we use 10 \times synthetic data. We also explore (1) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization and (2) privacy preservation when learning with synthetic data, and we show promising results. Apart from advancing the state of the art, our findings give insights into possible strategies for refining the training data synthesis pipeline. Our main contributions are:

- A principled distribution matching framework for training data synthesis, which emphasizes two foundational aspects that make synthetic data effective.

- Using the state-of-the-art text-to-image diffusion model, with a comprehensive analysis and refinement of its components, to design an effective training data synthesis strategy.

- Advancing the state of the art in training data synthesis for image classification tasks, and showing the advantages in OOD generalization and privacy preservation.

There are many image synthesis strategies, and deep generative models have received a lot of attention, mainly because they can produce high-fidelity images. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale annotated datasets [1,2] are essential in deep learning for image recognition, providing the comprehensive information that models need to discover patterns, learn representations, and generate accurate predictions. However, manually collecting such datasets is time-consuming and labor-intensive, and may raise privacy concerns. Given these challenges, training data synthesis offers a promising alternative to traditional data collection for augmenting or replacing original real datasets.

Among numerous image synthesis strategies, deep generative models have gained significant attention, primarily due to their ability to produce high-fidelity images. Early studies [3,4,5,6] use Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to synthesize annotated training data for image classification and segmentation. Recently, more works have focused on synthesizing training data with powerful diffusion models for self-supervised pre-training [7], transfer learning [8], domain generalization [9,10], and supervised image classification [11,12,13]. However, despite this extensive research, a notable performance gap remains between models trained on synthetic data and those trained on real data. A primary reason for this discrepancy is the misalignment between the synthetic and real data distributions, even when the diffusion model is trained on web-scale datasets, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a). While previous works have attempted to address this issue through heuristic-driven approaches such as prompt engineering [12,13] and expensive inversion approaches [6,14], these solutions are neither sufficient nor efficient. Furthermore, there are no theoretical frameworks that can adequately explain and analyze the efficacy of synthetic training data in a principled way.

To enhance the quality and utility of synthetic training data produced by deep generative models, we present a theoretical framework for training data synthesis from a distribution-matching perspective. Specifically, starting from the first principle of supervised learning [15,16], we recast training data synthesis as a distribution matching problem. This emphasizes two primary principles of synthetic data: (1) The distribution discrepancy between target and synthetic data, and (2) The cardinality of the training set.

Building on this foundation, we implement the framework on the state-of-the-art text-to-image diffusion model, Stable Diffusion [17], carefully analyzing and refining the training objectives, condition generation, and prior initialization to better align synthetic and target data distributions. We empirically validate our theoretical framework and synthesis method across diverse benchmarks covering various scenarios: (1) training exclusively with synthetic data, (2) augmenting the real training data, and (3) evaluating the scaling law between synthetic data and performance. In particular, for ImageNet1k classification using ResNet50 [18], training solely with synthetic data equivalent to 1 \times the original real data size yields a 70.9% Top1 classification accuracy, which increases to 76.0% with 10 \times synthetic data. We additionally explore (1) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization and (2) privacy preservation when learning with synthetic data, and present promising results. Beyond advancing the state of the art, our findings offer insights into potential strategies for refining the training data synthesis pipeline. Our primary contributions are as follows:

- Introducing a principled distribution matching framework for training data synthesis, which emphasizes two foundational aspects that drive the effectiveness of synthetic data.

- Employing the state-of-the-art text-to-image diffusion model, with a comprehensive analysis and refinement of its components, to design an effective training data synthesis strategy.

- Advancing the state of the art in training data synthesis for image classification tasks, while demonstrating advantages in OOD generalization and privacy preservation.
